title_angle: How the Giza pyramids shaped an ancient necropolis
facts: Giza is part of the Memphis and its Necropolis World Heritage site.
The site includes the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure.
Distinguish archaeological evidence from theories about construction.
The Step Pyramid of Djoser belongs to the Memphis necropolis.
The monument marks an important stage in the development of pyramid building.

title_angle: Life below the rock of Cappadocia
facts: The Göreme landscape contains rock-cut sanctuaries and underground settlements.
The area preserves traces of Byzantine art and history.

title_angle: The underground water system of Persian qanats
facts: Qanats use gently sloping underground channels to carry water by gravity.
The World Heritage property includes eleven qanats in Iran.

title_angle: How Petra endured in a desert landscape
facts: Petra was the capital of the Nabataeans.
Its setting includes rock-cut architecture and an extensive water management system.
Mohenjo-daro is a major archaeological site of the Indus civilization.
Its planned urban layout and drainage are important surviving evidence.
The eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Their remains preserve evidence of Roman urban life.

title_angle: The layered history of Islamic Cairo
facts: Historic Cairo was founded in the 10th century.
Its mosques, madrasas and other monuments reflect several centuries of Islamic history.
Cairo became the headquarters of the Fatimid Caliphate in 969 CE.
The city preserves mosques, madrasas, bathhouses and fountains.
Its surviving street plan and buildings also record Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods.
Samarra served as an Abbasid capital in the 9th century.
Its archaeological remains include monumental mosques and distinctive architecture.

title_angle: Ibn Battuta's travels and what his account can tell us
facts: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier in 1304.
He began a journey at about age 21, originally intending to make the hajj to Mecca.
His travels continued for almost 30 years and extended across North Africa, Asia and beyond.
After returning to Morocco in the early 1350s, he was commissioned to produce an account of his travels.
That account is commonly called the Rihla; distinguish its own claims from independently confirmed evidence.

title_angle: Ibn Sina's influence on medicine and philosophy
facts: Ibn Sina, also known as Avicenna, lived in the 10th and 11th centuries.
His Canon of Medicine became an influential medical work.
